title: OAuth, Headers, and MCP Tool Search

questions.prompt: You commit a .mcp.json so your team gets the same server. It needs a bearer token. Which entry keeps the secret out of git history?
options: "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${API_KEY}"} — the file holds the variable name, and expansion resolves it per machine at load time
"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer sk-live-abc123"} — remove it from the file in a later commit before the repo is public
"env": {"API_KEY": "sk-live-abc123"} on the server entry, since env values are not written to .mcp.json
Put the token in headersHelper, which runs as a shell command and so is never stored in the config
questions.explanation: Expansion runs in url, headers, command, args, and env, so ${API_KEY} in a committed file resolves from each machine's environment and the file itself holds no credential. Option B is the failure this prevents — once a secret is in history, deleting it later does not remove it. Option C is factually wrong; env values in .mcp.json are written to the file, which is exactly why expansion exists. Option D is a real mechanism but a shell command executes on load — trading a readable secret for executable config.

questions.prompt: A server exposes 60 tools and every session feels slower to start and /compact happens sooner. What does tool search, on by default, actually change here?
options: It caps each server at a smaller number of tools, dropping the rest permanently
It loads only tool names and server instructions at startup, deferring full descriptions until a query suggests a tool is relevant
It caches the tool definitions on disk so later sessions don't pay for them
It disables tools from servers you haven't used in the last few sessions
questions.explanation: Tool search changes when descriptions load, not which tools exist — the full list is always reachable, just found by searching descriptions when something looks relevant, so startup cost stays small as servers multiply. Option A is a cap that doesn't exist. Option C describes a caching layer that isn't the mechanism, and it wouldn't help the first session anyway. Option D is invented; unused servers aren't retired.

questions.prompt: You mark a whole 60-tool server with alwaysLoad true because you use three of its tools most days. What did you actually buy?
options: Faster tool discovery, since everything is visible without a search step
All 60 tool definitions in context on every turn of every session, plus a startup that now waits for that server to connect
Correctness — deferred tools can be missed, while always-loaded ones cannot
Nothing until the tools are first used, after which they stay pinned
questions.explanation: alwaysLoad exempts a server from deferral, which means every definition is resident in the window every turn — a standing context cost — and startup waits for the server so the first prompt has its tools. That is the right trade only for one or two tools you reach for constantly; pinning 60 to use 3 spends the budget Lesson 32 told you to protect. Option C is the tempting justification and it is wrong: deferral changes discovery, not availability.

questions.prompt: One MCP tool returns a 200,000-character schema dump. At the default threshold, what does the model actually receive?
options: The first 50,000 characters, with the rest dropped
A file reference to the persisted full result, not the 200,000 characters inline
The full result inline, with older parts dropped from the window by compaction later
An error, because a tool result cannot exceed the limit
questions.explanation: Oversized results aren't truncated — they're persisted and replaced in the conversation by a reference, so the model reads a pointer and can work from the file. That distinction matters: a truncated schema is a wrong schema, whereas a file reference is a redirect the agent can follow. Per-tool _meta anthropic/maxResultSizeChars raises the threshold for that one tool, scoped rather than session-wide.
